# Aristotelian Foundations of Temporality and Perception: Motion, Time, and the Unity of Consciousness

## 1.a. Aristotle's Understanding of Motion

Aristotle's conception of motion (kinesis) represents a foundational departure from Platonic metaphysics, establishing movement not as participation in eternal forms but as a fundamental mode of being itself. Indeed, Heidegger's interpretation reveals that "kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 288), indicating that motion constitutes the very being of beings rather than merely describing their accidental properties. This ontological priority of motion emerges through Aristotle's sophisticated understanding of the relationship between potentiality (dynamis) and actuality (entelecheia), where kinesis functions as the actualization of potential being precisely as potential. The complexity of Aristotelian motion becomes evident when we examine Heidegger's analysis of the Physics, particularly the definition that "Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 322). This formulation  ambiguity between active and passive dimensions of movement, suggesting that motion cannot be reduced to simple mechanical causation. Rather, kinesis reveals the fundamental interconnectedness of beings in their temporal unfolding; thus, motion emerges as a phenomenon that exceeds the traditional subject-object dichotomy by demonstrating how being-moved and moving-others constitute a unified ontological structure. Furthermore, Heidegger's morphosyntactical  Aristotle's Greek formulation preserves essential ambiguities that scholastic interpretations subsequently obscured. The middle voice construction in Greek allows for the recognition that "passivity and activity are fundamentally interanimate" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27), revealing motion as neither purely active nor passive but as a mode of being that transcends such binary distinctions. This understanding proves crucial for comprehending how temporal awareness emerges through the soul's participation in the very structure of kinesis itself. ## Aristotle on Time

Aristotle's analysis of time in Physics IV establishes temporal experience as fundamentally connected to the soul's capacity to measure and discriminate motion. Time, according to Aristotle, exists as the number or measure of motion with respect to before and after, but this measurement requires the presence of a counting soul that can hold together past and present moments in unified awareness. The temporal structure thus emerges not as an objective container for events but through the soul's active participation in the discrimination of temporal phases. The relationship between time and motion reveals itself as more complex than simple succession of discrete moments; indeed, temporal awareness requires the soul's capacity to maintain continuity across change while simultaneously recognizing distinction. As Bowin observes in his analysis, "the discriminating power and the time of its exercise must be one and undivided" (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, p. 17), indicating that temporal perception involves a synthetic unity that cannot be reduced to mere mechanical registration of sequential events. This synthetic character of temporal awareness points toward the essential role of phantasia in organizing temporal experience. The measurement of time necessarily involves the soul's capacity to hold together what is no longer present (the past) with what is not yet present (the future) through the mediating function of the now-moment. Thus, temporal experience reveals the soul's fundamental transcendence of mere present-at-hand existence, establishing human being as essentially temporal in character. This temporality manifests not as subjective projection onto objective time but as the very condition for the possibility of encountering beings in their temporal unfolding. ## The Relation Between Motion and Time

The intimate connection between motion and time in Aristotelian physics reveals temporal awareness as grounded in the soul's participation in kinetic processes rather than in abstract mathematical measurement. Motion provides the ontological foundation for temporal discrimination because change itself makes possible the recognition of before and after relationships that constitute temporal structure. Accordingly, time emerges as neither independent of motion nor simply identical to motion but as the measured aspect of motion that becomes accessible through the soul's discriminating activity. Heidegger's interpretation illuminates how this relationship transcends mechanical causation by revealing kinesis as "entelecheia tou dynamei poietikou kai pathetikou he toiouton" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26), which indicates the fulfillment of what can act and what can be acted upon as such. This  motion involves the actualization of relational capacities rather than the displacement of discrete objects through space. Hence, temporal awareness emerges through the soul's participation in these relational dynamics, suggesting that time and motion constitute a unified phenomenon accessible through embodied engagement rather than detached observation. The soul's capacity to experience time thus depends upon its fundamental character as being-in-motion, where the discriminating power that recognizes temporal relationships participates in the very kinetic structure it seeks to understand. This participatory character of temporal awareness reveals why Aristotle's analysis cannot be reduced to modern mechanistic conceptions of time as uniform duration; rather, temporal experience emerges through the soul's attunement to the qualitative rhythms of natural processes, establishing temporality as fundamentally ecological rather than merely chronological. ## Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Aristotelian aisthēsis (perception) provides the foundation for temporal awareness through the soul's capacity to discriminate present sensory content while retaining traces of past impressions. Perception, however, cannot account for the full range of temporal experience, particularly the soul's capacity to anticipate future possibilities and organize complex temporal relationships. Indeed, aisthēsis functions primarily in the present moment, though it establishes the sensory foundation upon which more complex temporal syntheses depend. The limitations of direct perceptual awareness become evident when we consider Heidegger's analysis of fear (phobos) in Aristotelian rhetoric, where "fear becomes present to us not by direct experience, aisthesis, but through our imagination, phantasia; fancies replace sensations as stimulus" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). This observation reveals that temporal awareness, particularly future-directed awareness, requires capacities that exceed immediate sensory registration. The soul's engagement with temporal relationships thus involves a complex interplay between present perception and imaginative synthesis. The temporal character of aisthēsis itself emerges through the soul's capacity to organize sensory manifolds into coherent perceptual wholes, a process that requires holding together successive impressions in unified awareness. This synthetic activity points toward the essential role of phantasia in mediating between immediate sensory content and the complex temporal relationships that constitute meaningful experience. Thus, while perception provides the material foundation for temporal awareness, it necessarily involves imaginative synthesis that transcends the mere registration of present-at-hand sensory data. ## Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Phantasia emerges in Aristotelian psychology as the crucial mediating faculty that enables the soul to organize temporal experience by synthesizing present perceptions with retained impressions and anticipated possibilities. Unlike mere reproductive imagination, phantasia functions as an active power that creates new temporal syntheses by combining and recombining sensory materials in ways that transcend immediate perceptual presentation. 15). The temporal function of phantasia becomes particularly evident in rhetorical contexts, where effective discourse must coordinate past precedents, present circumstances, and future consequences in persuasive synthesis. As Heidegger observes, Aristotelian rhetoric involves "a radically timeful practice of changes, alterations designed to take account of past, present, and future in the respective genres of judicial, epideictic, and deliberative oratory" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). This temporal coordination requires imaginative capacities that can hold together what is absent (past and future) with what is present in unified awareness, establishing phantasia as essential to practical temporal navigation. This projective character reveals phantasia as fundamentally futural in orientation, enabling the soul to transcend mere reactive response to present stimuli by anticipating and preparing for possible developments. Hence, phantasia establishes the foundation for deliberative activity by creating temporal syntheses that make rational choice possible within the flux of changing circumstances. ## Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's engagement with Aristotelian philosophy reveals fundamental insights into the temporal structure of human existence that traditional metaphysical interpretations have obscured. His  Aristotelian concepts, particularly kinesis and the pathē (passions), anticipate existential themes that become explicit in Being and Time. Indeed, Heidegger recognizes that "the ontological significance of the passions lies in our capacity for change, the Veränderlichkeit of Being" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115), revealing temporal mutability as essential to human existence rather than accidental to it. The Heideggerian  Aristotelian kinesis transcends mechanical motion by revealing being as fundamentally temporal and relational. This reading challenges traditional metaphysical categories by showing how motion constitutes a way of being rather than merely describing changes in substance. Accordingly, Heidegger's analysis reveals temporal awareness as grounded in the soul's participation in kinetic processes rather than in abstract theoretical cognition, establishing embodied temporal engagement as primary. Most significantly, Heidegger's interpretation reveals how Aristotelian concepts anticipate the dissolution of traditional subject-object dichotomies by showing how human being emerges through relational engagement rather than substantial isolation. The pathē function as "dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115), establishing temporal awareness as fundamentally intersubjective and contextual. This relational understanding of temporality reveals how Aristotelian insights contribute to contemporary philosophical efforts to think beyond representationalist frameworks toward more ecological and participatory approaches to temporal experience. Thus, Heidegger's creative appropriation of Aristotelian concepts reveals their contemporary relevance for understanding temporal awareness as emerging through embodied engagement rather than detached observation; this interpretation establishes the foundation for thinking temporality as fundamentally ecological, relational, and participatory rather than merely chronological or mechanical. The Aristotelian legacy, as mediated through Heideggerian interpretation, accordingly provides crucial resources for contemporary efforts to understand temporal awareness as emerging through what Rickert calls "ambient" engagement with environing contexts rather than through isolated subjective synthesis. ---
